Canadian Camping 









EDITORIAL 


We Believe ... 


. . . that* . . . through our efforts . . . 
the personality of each individual child 
and adult may be genuinely enriched. 

Upon this premise, directors in “po¬ 
tential-packed” children’s camps from 
coast to coast are basing their plans 
for the coming season! 

For many, the winter has provided 
periods for quiet meditation . . . for 
searching discussion . . . and for care¬ 
ful and unhurried formulation of ob¬ 
jectives 

Notable among these groups is the 
program committee of Vancouver 
Y.M.C.A.’s Gamp Elphinstone, who, 
with Chairman, Lome E. Brown, and 
Camp Director, David T. Yard, have 
developed the following statements . . . 
stars for charting a straight course to¬ 
wards a fruitful camping summer. 

We believe 

—that campers should quickly and 
thoroughly acquire skills in caring 
for themselves and others. Thus we 
will provide trained and skilled 
counsellors and staff insofar as is 
possible. 

—that counsellors should be mature 
and skilled persons in dealing with 
and understanding boys. Thus we 
will raise the minimum age and the 
qualifications for counsellors as high 
as possible. 

—that campers and counsellors should 
share in the planning of the camp 


programme. Thus provision will be 
made for the campers and counsel¬ 
lors to participate in programme 
planning. 

—that the recreational and education¬ 
al aspects of camp should be the 
means to an end, . . . not the end in 
themselves. Thus all programme will 
be planned with the idea of what it 
will do for the individual. 

—that parents are important to camp 
and should therefore be welcomed in 
the camp setting. Thus Parents’ Days 
will be encouraged in keeping with 
good administrative procedures. 

—that campcraft and naturelore, de¬ 
veloped through out-tripping, are 
the cornerstones of the camp pro¬ 
gramme. Thus skilled personnel will 
be made available, out-trip sites pro¬ 
cured, and out-trip equipment in¬ 
cluded and maintained in the camp 
inventories. 

—that crafts as they are related to out¬ 
door living and the camp programme 
in general, are important. Thus we 
will provide an adequate shop where 
materials and tools will be available 
to campers under trained leadership. 

—that games and sports should be part 
of the camp programme. Thus we 
will provide an improved campus on 
which activities can be carried on 
in a satisfying way, as well as im¬ 
proved recreational equipment and 
facilities. 

continued on page 33 


Toronto , Canada, June , 1956 


11 




A Public Mi*alth Inspector 

Looks 

at Sommer Lamps 

By K. E. B. Symons., 

Ontario Department of Health 


Summer camps vary widely in size, 
duration, facilities and programme, to 
encompass pioneer, religious, charitable, 
and luxury types, with various degrees 
of intergrading. The aim of all pro¬ 
grammes is to train the camper along 
some line which invariably includes 
good health habits. Illness and : accident 
are two certain spoilers of the pleasures 
of summer camping. 

Through the medium of the Summer 
Camp Regulations and periodic camp 
inspections, the Ontario Department of 
Health endeavours to guide the camp 
operator to obtain satisfactory sanitary 
operations and physical development. 
Individual development, as opposed to 
standardization, is promoted. 

Operator 

In Ontario the summer camp 
operator is required to hold a license. 
It is his responsibility to see that the 
Regulations are observed. The inspector 
is anxious to conduct the camp in¬ 
spection with the operator or camp 
director because this personal contact 
promotes mutual understanding, con¬ 
structive discussion, and a better basis 
for assessing the camp. 

Site 

The nature of the camp and the 
proposed programme dictate certain 
conditions of the site. Briefly, the area 
should be well drained, and of sufficient 
size to allow for physical structure and 
ample playground. Topographic and 


soil features are very important. A light 
or sandy soil is desirable since it drains 
quickly, and facilitates the construction 
of waste disposal works. The availability 
of water and accessibility of the site 
are two other major considerations. 

Medical Care 

Campers and staff, particlarly food 
handlers, should have a medical 
examination prior to or immediately 
upon arrival at camp. While the initial 
purpose is to exclude those having 
communicable diseases, information is 
also supplied concerning special care 
required by any camper. Adequate 
medical care should be conveniently 
available to the camp. Resident nurses 
and doctors are hired by some camps 
with appropriate infirmary facilities. 
Smaller groups should make a contact 
with a local physician and provide first 
aid equipment on the site. 

Isolation quarters should be provided 
away from regular eating and sleeping 
accommodation. 

Water Supply 

A safe, adequate water supply is 
essential. Auxiliary supplies must be 
potable. Well and spring supplies should 
be so constructed and protected as to 
prevent contamination by surface water, 
splashage, or other means. A dipping 
vessel is a potential source of contami¬ 
nation. Either a pump or an overflow 
should be employed. Priming of a pump 
may also cause adverse analyses. 


12 


Canadian Camping 


When water is hauled into camp 
in auxiliary vessels, chlorination in the 
dispensing unit is required. 

All surface water supplies and ad¬ 
verse ground water supplies must be 
chlorinated. Whether a commercial 
chlorinator is employed on a pressure 
system or batch chlorination in dispens¬ 
ing units, control by the ortho-tolodine 
test is recommended. A chlorine residual 
of 0.2 to 0.3 parts per million should 
be secured when the sample is tested 
after fifteen minutes’ contact between 
the water and the chlorine. This con¬ 
centration is sufficient to disinfect clear 
waters without producing a taste. 

A chlorine outfit suitable for batch 
chlorination of water at a small camp 
may be purchased from the Ontario 
Department of Health. Commercial 
comparators are suggested for control 
of chlorination in a pressure system. 
However, a suitable temporary kit is 
available from the Department. 

The submission of water samples for 
bacteriological analysis prior to and 
during the camp period is advised. 
Sample bottles may be obtained from 
the local Medical Officer of Health, or 
directly from the Central Laboratory, 
360 Christie Street, Toronto, or one 
of the eighteen Regional Branches or 
Associated Laboratories throughout the 
Province. 

For dispensing drinking water, a 
sanitary fountain on a pressure system 
is ideal. The use of a common drinking 
cup is not permitted. Single paper 
service at a covered tap-type dispenser 
is suggested for camps without a pres¬ 
sure system. 

Natural ice should not be employed 
for direct cooling of drinking water. 

Sanitary Facilities 

Toilet accommodation should be 
provided on the basis of one toilet seat 


for each ten females, and each twenty 
males, and one urinal for each fifteen 
males. Flush toilets, septic toilets, and 
pit, pail or vault privies are all com¬ 
monly employed. The plumbing of flush 
toilet systems should comply with the 
Ontario Plumbing Regulations. Ap¬ 
proval of septic tank disposal systems 
should be obtained from the local 
Medical Officer of Health. 

Buildings housing sanitary con¬ 
veniences should be of sound construc¬ 
tion, well ventilated, and properly fitted 
with screens and a self-closing door. 
Pit privies should be deep, dry, venti¬ 
lated, and tight against flies and 
rodents. Separate urinals are suggested 
for boys’ camps. Covers are required 
for toilet seats which must be scrubbed 
daily with a cleansing or disinfecting 
solution. 

A larvicide should be used in pit 
privies. A minimum earth cover of nine 
inches is required when burying night 
soil. 

Ablution Facilities 

Specific ablution facilities should be 
provided at every permanent camp site. 
These facilities may vary from portable 
hand basins to ablution tables or huts 
where a pressure water system is 
available. 

Safe water and sanitary waste dis¬ 
posal should be provided for teeth 
cleaning operations. 

Liquid Waste Disposal 

Disposal systems are required for 
liquid wastes from- kitchen, ablution 
and flush toilet operations. These may 
be handled individually or collectively. 
A grease trap should be provided for 
pre-treatment of kitchen wastes. Assist¬ 
ance in planning septic tank systems is 
available from the Local or Provincial 
Health Departments. 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1956 


13 



Where w,et pits are used, these should 
be of adequate size and fitted with 
tight covers. 

Refuse 

Garbage and rubbish may be disposed 
of by a collection service, burial, inci¬ 
neration, or a combination of these 
methods. Garbage should be covered 
immediately upon dumping. Some 
measures may be necessary to prevent 
wildlife from feeding on the garbage. 
Chicken wire will control digging. 

Metal receptacles with tight-fitting 
covers'are essential at the kitchen, and 
throughout the camp area. Separate 
cans for wet garbage, combustible 
materials, and rubbish facilitate dis¬ 
posal. 

The kitchen garbage cans should be 
washed regularly and stored in a 
manner that provides fly protection, and 
screens appearance. 

Sleeping Quarters 

Where tents are used, a minimum 
floo'r space of thirty square feet per 
cSfftjber is recommended. In cabins, 
dbfmitories, etc., a minimum of three 
hundred cubic feet of air space per 
camper should be provided. Single 
beds with minimum spacing for single 
cots or bedrolls and double decker 
bunks""df eighteen inches and thirty 
inches Respectively are required. 

Ventilation and screening are im¬ 
portant. Peak ventilation is particularly 
effective. 

Two exits are necessary for accom¬ 
modation above the ground floor. 

Food Control 

A review of the Eating Establish¬ 
ment Regulations is advised when 
planning permanent kitchen and dining 


room facilities. The construction of the 
building and equipment should facili¬ 
tate cleaning and general good house¬ 
keeping. Ventilation and screening are 
important. 

Refrigerated storage below 50° F is 
essential for perishable foods, particular¬ 
ly meat and milk products. Special care 
must be exercised in the storage and 
use of left-overs. Only pasteurized milk 
is permissible in a summer camp. 

A minimum programme for dish¬ 
washing includes a warm wash and a 
final chlorine disinfecting rinse. Prefer¬ 
able methods include: 

(a) Wash in a detergent solution at 
110° F, 

(b) Rinse in clear water at 110° F, 
and— 

(c) Sterilize by: (1) a hot water rinse 
at 170°F for two minutes; (2) a 
chlorine rinse at 100 p.p.m. for two 
minutes or (3) a quaternary 
ammonium rinse at 200 p.p.m. for 
two minutes. 

Test papers for chlorine or quater¬ 
nary ammonium compounds should be 
obtained if these products are used. 
The hot water method with racks 
permits air drying of dishes. The 
dishes should be stored in a dust and 
fly free manner. 

Food handlers must be meticulous in 
their personal cleanliness and habits. 
Persons with colds, infections, or hand 
cuts should not handle food. 

Bathing 

Bathing should be closely supervised. 
Use of restricted and classified swim¬ 
ming areas are advised. Appropriate 
life saving equipment should be 
maintained. In children’s camps, an 
adult trained in life saving procedures 
should be in charge. 

continued on page 4 6

Canadian Camping 


AMONG 

OURSELVES 

Helen MacKey Hall-Wood 



Dorothy Percival 


“Camping in the Laurentians” is a 
familiar phrase to thousands of girls 
who have had that delightful experi¬ 
ence. The phrase has a particular 
appeal to the hundreds of campers and 
counsellors who have been associated 
with Camp Ouareau and Miss Dorothy 
Percival—“Miss Percy” as she is affec¬ 
tionately called. 

The love and esteem in which 
Miss Percy is held by her camp friends 
could be no better exemplified than by 
their presence at a Reception and 
Presentation held in her honour in 
Montreal on the eve of her retirement 
from Camp Ouareau this past year. A 
period of 29 years was represented as 
Ouareauites came from near and far 
to pay her tribute. 

Miss Percival was born and educated 
in Montreal. In her youth she was in¬ 
troduced to the out-of-doors by her 
father, an ardent nature lover, who 
made it a habit while on fishing trips 


to the Gatineau Hills, to bring along 
his daughters. This was Miss Percival’s 
initiation in camping, an early interest 
which was later to become her vocation. 

Miss Percival commenced her career 
as a teacher with the Westmount 
School Board, Montreal. Concurrently 
she worked as a volunteer at the Old 
Brewery Mission Camp. Resigning from 
teaching in 1922, she joined the staff 
of the Montreal Y.W.C.A., where she 
served for two years as Girl’s Work 
Secretary. During the summers, the job 
involved the directing of the Y.W.C.A.’s 
Camp Oolahwan at St. Margaret’s, 
Quebec. 

After a trip abroad, Miss Percival 
returned to teaching and spent three 
summers as a counsellor at Camp 
Ouareau which had been established by

Miss Mabel C. Jamieson. Miss Percival’s 
contribution to the Camp was quite 
evident, for the next year she became 
associate director of this girls’ camp. 
As the seasons progressed, camping 
developed into a full time interest and 
in 1937 she took over the Directorship 
of Camp Ouareau. During the next few 
years, Miss Percival contributed a great 
amount of her time and effort as an 
active member on the Quebec and 
Canadian Camping Associations. She 
was the President of the Quebec 
Association for two years and Member¬ 
ship Chairman on the Board of the 
Canadian Camping Association. Her 
participation in conferences and con¬ 
ventions and for years her lectures on 
camping given to the McGill University 
Health and Physical Education students, 
were a regular part of her busy 
schedule. Moreover, her ability as a 
group leader gave her many opportu¬ 
nities to impart her knowledge and 
experience to young people in the 
Church, the Sunday Schools and girls’ 
work departments of the Y.W.C.A. 

Those privileged to have been 
associated with Miss Percy at Ouareau 
consider the experience to be one of 
the finest in their lives — an inspiration 
in leadership and accomplishment. It 
is not unusual to witness high personal 
standarls, but it is a rare experience to 
see them instilled in others. Miss Perci¬ 
val as a Camp Director was able to 
transfer her enthusiasm in such a way 
as to engender the utmost pleasure and 
pride in work well done. At the same 
time she was able to take a personal 
interest in the problems and activities 
of individual campers. This interest in 
them accounted for their love and 
loyalty to her, for it is human nature, 
especially evident in children, to appre¬ 
ciate recognition and attention. 

Nothing at Ouareau was left to 
chance. Preparedness, forethought and

Canadian Camping 















THE 

HOMESICK 

BOY 

Helen Gruden r.n. 

Camp Nurse, 

Haliburton Scout Reserve. 


Of all the illnesses that can beset a 
boy at camp, homesickness can be the 
most disquieting. Fortunately, the 
appearance of this disease is the ex¬ 
ception rather than the rule during the 
life of a busy camper; nevertheless, 
when it does occur, it requires treat¬ 
ment as does the sore throat or clob¬ 
bered toe. 

Mild forms of homesickness are dealt 
with in the majority of cases success¬ 
fully by experienced counsellors. The 
techniques used are well described in 
the basic camping textbooks. However, 
in a few . cases these methods do not 
work and the camper usually arrives 
at camp sick parade complaining of 
physical symptoms such as headache, 
abdominal cramps, muscular pains, 
dizziness and so on. 

The first step in these cases is a 
careful examination by the camp doctor 
to rule out the possibility of actual 
physical basis for the symptoms. One 
should not dismiss these cases lightly: 
a mistaken diagnosis of homesickness 
may end in tragedy. In our camp, they 


are admitted to the camp hospital for 
observation. 

On my first encounter with this 
disease, I was in sympathy with the 
T.L.C. treatment (Tender loving care) 
recommended highly during the pe¬ 
diatric part of my training as a necessity 
in the management of any sick young¬ 
ster. With this foremost in mind, the 
homesick boy was given my complete 
attention, along with comic books in 
abundance, soft bed, games, visitors at 
will, and food on a tray. What hap¬ 
pened? The homesickness appeard to be 
cured, but actually it was only mis¬ 
placed. The boy still wasn’t ready to 
return to a normal camp life. 

Obviously, this was the wrong 
approach, so I admitted failure and re¬ 
sorted to a recipe highly recommended 
by our Camp staff . . . and it worked. 

The bed was still soft, but comic 
books, games, visitors, and even food 
were removed from the routine. Upon 
admission to camp hospital, the boy 
was settled in bed and given a large jug 
of apple juice and a glass. He was 
told that this jug (refilled as desired) 
will be his only source of nourishment 
until his disturbing symptoms have 
disappeared. The apple juice routine 
combined with isolation, although 
sounding a bit rugged, produce rapid 
results in at least the disappearance 
of the aches and pains. 

The initial step accomplished, a very 
large full diet is begun and a period of 
rehabilitation begins. There are always 
several odd jobs at camp for which 
there are never enough hands—paint¬ 
ing, building, gardening, to mention 
only a few. Working with a staff mem¬ 
ber, the boy works on the particular 
occupation that appeals to him. A day 
or two of this adult working atmosphere, 

continued on page 23 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1956

OPERATION 

MARATHON 


Nancy Porter, 

Programme Head 
Camp Tanamakoon 


The successful camp programme 
must include, not only a well-balanced 
schedule of activities, but also an 
occasional relief or change from that 
routine. Most camps have special days 
which have become tradition to their 
campers, and are eagerly awaited events 
of the summer. However, new ideas for 
such days are always welcome, and here 
is one which proved successful at our 
camp last year, and could, with varia¬ 
tions, be adapted for use in any camping 
situation. We called it Marathon Day. 

Actually, it was only half a day, 
occupying the morning and ending in 
time for general swim before the noon 
meal. Because the older campers are 
so eager to participate in the various 
activities, we have found that for 
regattas, United Nations Days, in fact 
almost any interruption of the regular 
programme, half a day is sufficient. 

Marathon Day provided a means of 
letting the younger campers participate 


on equal terms with the eldest (some¬ 
thing they dearly love) and also gave 
prominence to camp activities often 
overlooked in competitions which seem, 
inevitably, to centre around the water¬ 
front. 

Before the events are outlined, some 
description of the organization required 
should be given. Very little was needed 
in our case, since the camp was already 
divided into six teams, including 
campers from each age group or tribe 
who elect a captain and compete in 
various events over the month. These 
teams, then, were our competitors, and 
the team captains, campers from the 
oldest tribe arranged the participation 
of their own members with the help of 
their counsellor-advisers. 

The staff of each activity was respons¬ 
ible for the direction of the events 
concerning their department. Each 
team had its list of events, which in 


18 


Canadian Camping 




every case, began and ended on the 
front dock. There were three routes, 
meaning that each team started with 
another and followed the same route, 
although any team might 1 pass another 
along the way. Since all started at the 
same time, the first to complete the 
course was the winner. As each com¬ 
petitor finished, she could follow her 
team, so the whole camp was gathered 
at the dock for the finish. 

A bugle told us to take up our posi¬ 
tions; another, ten minutes later, or¬ 
dered START. Let’s follow Team One 
around the course. 

Camper 1 must throw a ring buoy 
(as in Red Cross Tests) past 
camper 2 who is treading water 
some 20 feet off shore, and pull 
her to the dock. 

Camper 2 then runs to 3 at the 
shallow end of the pool. 

Camper 3 swims the length of the 
pool and runs to the tower. 

Camper 4 jumps from the tower and 
swims to the raft. 

Camper 5 is waiting at the raft in a 
canoe, and must do standing 
paddling to Cree Point (see map). 

Camper 6 hammers three nails 
through two boards and then 

Camper 7 must remove them and 
run to the shore where 

Campers 8 and 9 wait in their canoe, 
and paddle to Dawendena. 

Camper 10 at Dawendena, must lay 
and light a fire to bum a string 
suspended above it. This permits 

Camper 11 to start looking for a list 
of plants which she must collect 
before. 


Camper 12 can orienteer a course 
which will bring her to the theatre. 

Camper 13, waiting at the theatre, 
gives a “reading” to satisfy the 
dramatics counsellor, and 

Camper 14 runs all the way to the 
craft shop. 

Camper 15 punches and laces leather 
to make a little autograph book, 
then to the tennis court. 

Camper 16 must serve correctly eight 
balls which 

Camper 17 is able to return across 
the net. Both then run to the ar¬ 
chery range. 

Camper 18 ready with bow and 
arrows, shoots until she has a score 
of 25, then runs to the Lodge. 

Camper 19, at the piano, must play 
the two octaves of the scale of C 
major before going to the canoeing 
dock. 

Camper 20 paddles out a set distance 
and comes back to shore by gun¬ 
wale bobbing. Docking her canoe 
with assistance, she runs to the 
sailing dock. 

Camper 21 rigs dinghy properly, and 

Camper 22 stows it. 

All this time Team Two has been 
following the same route while Three 
and Four, who started at the sailing 
dock, will finish at the ring-buoy throw, 
and Five and Six, starting with the 
tower jump, end with pool swim. From 
the smallest nine year old to the most 
accomplished camper of sixteen sum¬ 
mers, all have helped (or hindered) 
their team. All are looking forward to 
another Marathon Day. Perhaps you 
will try one too. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, June 3 1956

WHODUZIT? 


Who sets up the camp program? 

This month, Whoduzit moves into 
the vital realm of “programming”. 
However, it should be stated at the 
outset that this is not a discussion of 
“why” we program, nor of “what 
kind” of program. Rather, we shall 
content ourselves with an analysis of 
“Whoduzit” in one camp situation. If 
in reading, one discerns that a ‘philo¬ 
sophy of programming” permeates the 
operational structure, we can only plead 
that to the degree it is evidenced, we 
have found philosophy and structure 
inseparable. 

1, The Basic Philosophy of Pro- 
r gramming 

is determined and clearly and ar¬ 
ticulately stated by the Gamp 
Committee and Director. 

2. Over-all Program outline 

is set up in advance by the Di¬ 
rector and Senior staff members. 

—This planning involves which of 
the “special’ events that campers 
expect annually will occur, at 
what periods. 

—This advance planning enables 
the Director to purchase certain 
materials that may be required 
and to contact certain resource 
persons whose presence at camp 
may be desirable at some particu¬ 
lar time. 

—This “outline” is further dis¬ 
cussed and changed or confirmed 


-W. E. (Ted) Yard 

Y.M. C. A. Camp Pivecrest 

r ^ 

by the staff at the pre-camp 
training conference — it may in¬ 
volve the placing of about six 
highlight events throughout the 
summer. * 

3. Instruction Groups 

—The basic planning for these 
takes place during the winter and 
is furthered at the pre-camp 
training conference when those 
who are to assume instructor roles 
discuss what they hope to 
achieve in each activity, and how 
they hope to do it. 

—In a camp of two main “Sec¬ 
tions” — one has the use of in¬ 
struction facilities and staff in 
the morning and the other in 
the afternoon. 

—Changes in these instruction 
groups, i.e. what groups, how 
conducted, how many chiMren 
etc., are discussed by instructors, 
counsellors and senior staff in 
evening meetings. 

—When the time arrives for in¬ 
struction groups, each child 
chooses the group he goes to. The 
section head keeps track of where 
children are, and tries to help 
them make decisions which will 
result in a well-rounded experi¬ 
ence for them. 

—Beginners swim instruction is 
not among these free-choice pro¬ 
grams, but is scheduled at a time 
when all non-swimmers can take 
part. 


20 


Canadian Camping 




4. Cabin Group Activities 

The basic pattern of Instruction 
Groups for one half the day pro¬ 
vides a good opportunity to 
schedule cabin group activities for 
the other half. These activities are 
as wide in variety as the interests 
and imagination of campers and 
counsellors. There are few restric¬ 
tions and clearances are made 
with Section Directors. 

5. Inter-cabin events are planned by 
campers and counsellors and clear¬ 
ed through Section Directors. 

6. Section Events 

involving six or seven cabin 
groups in one section are fre¬ 
quently planned by 

(a) Camper Council — with rep¬ 
resentatives from each cabin 
who meet regularly. 

(b) Counsellors — who get “in¬ 
spirations” at their evening 
sessions, and talk them over 
with the boys the next day. 

7. Canoe Trips and Hikes 

The decision to go on these is 
made by the cabin group, and 
from that point on they are as¬ 
sisted with all phases of the plan¬ 
ning (including making up their 
menus, choosing route, etc.) by a 
member of the out-trip staff. 

8. Waterfront Programs 

are frequently developed at the re¬ 
quest of campers and counsellors, 
but this program is inevitably 
planned in detail and carried 
through by the waterfront spe¬ 
cialists. 


9. All Camp 

events are carried through by 
special committees struck off to 
develop each event, i.e. Chapel 
Committee”; “Annual Games 
Committee”; ‘Circus Committee”. 

—These committees have repre¬ 
sentation from the whole camp 
community. 

—The same procedure on a smal¬ 
ler scale is used for sectional 
events such as Stunt Nights, Ama¬ 
teur Nights. 

10. Clearances 

regarding program and use of 
equipment are made daily through 
the Senior Staff Cabinet consisting 
of Camp Director, Section Heads, 
Waterfront, Outtrips, Music and 
Crafts Directors. There is no over¬ 
all “program director” in this par¬ 
ticular situation. 

11. Staff Social Events 

are planned by a Staff Committee 
set up for the specific purpose of 
planning the event. 

Outlining a “framework” such as 
this, leaves out the innumerable “indi¬ 
vidual” factors which section heads 
and counsellors consider in providing 
quite “unscheduled” kinds of pro¬ 
gram and leadership for boys where 
needs indicate a deviation from the 
planned program opportunities. 

The Camp Director’s function here 
is not to develop program, but rather 
to give guidance and counsel to en¬ 
sure that all the things that happen to 
people at camp are consistent with the 
over-all philosophy. 

— • 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1956

CREATIVE ART 
AT 

SUMMER CAMP 


By Frances Gage 
Camp Tanamakoon 



Hurricane Hazel furnished us, this 
summer at Tanamakoon, with a fine 
cedar log for a new totem pole. The 
pole was an ideal project for camp. 
The material was provided by the 
woods, our tools were simple, and there 
was no lack of energy and enthusiasm. 

It is very rewarding to see what can 
be done in creative art at camp. Gamp 
is a special place where children learn 
to live with nature. Time is short in 
this unique situation, and any activities 
that can be done just as well at home 
in the city have little meaning. We 
must remember, however, that no one 
comes to camp to learn to be an artist. 
There are places better equipped and 
staffed for such aspirants. Creative art, 
therefore, should be put in its proper 
place, which is that of enriching our 
lives, and complementing our sur¬ 
roundings. 


Materials should be kept to a mini¬ 
mum. Of course, we cannot, as the 
Indians did, paint our home-made 
pigments on hand-prepared skins, or 
carve wood and slate with stone 
chisels, for we have neither the time 
nor the technique. But with a few basic 
supplies, satisfying results can be 
obtained. 

Sketching is one art form that lends 
itself to life at camp, ‘ Here*’ the child 
learns to observe nature in yet another 
way; the way peculiar only to the 
artist. All that is required in the way 
of materials is a board, manilla paper, 
and pencil, chalk or charcoal. After 
some instruction in basic design and 
composition, the child sees the forest 
anew, as a place alive with depths, 
colours, shades and shadows. 

continued on page 25 


22 


Canadian Camping 


continued from page ll 

and the fun-life of camp beckons him 
back. He himself makes the request to 
return to his campsite and enjoy the 
remainder of his stay. 

The theory behind this method of 
handling homesickness is that a boy 
arriving in camp has in his recent ex¬ 
perience two situations only: the 
familiar, protected, homelife which he 
has just left, and the strange, new, camp 
life which he has just met. He may 
prefer the former so strongly that actual 


illness may appear to be present in an 
unconscious attempt to return home. 
The routine described above adds a 
third and considerably less desirable 
situation which leads the child to seek 
the lesser evil: life back on the camp¬ 
site. After the transition period the 
activity of camp wipes away his original 
fears and all is well. 

This method has been used quite 
successfully in our camp and has been 
a solution to the problem of handling 
this type of homesickness.

Canadian Camping 




continued from page 22 

To the boy or girl who is especially 
gifted, sketching is a very valuable basic 
training. It provides some of the basic 
steps towards all branches of art, such 
as painting, sculpture and architecture, 
which he might study further at studio 
or school. Ability, however, is not a 
prerequisite to the enjoyment of sketch¬ 
ing, or other activities such as carving 
or whittling. 

Everyone likes to whittle. Work with 
wood, whittling or carving seems a 
natural thing to do in the woods. The 
necessary material is usually readily 
available, in many varieties, hard and 
soft. For our purpose, we might choose 
basswood, white pine or cedar. Bass¬ 
wood for its soft, even texture; pine 
and cedar for their straight grain. The - 
latter requires careful handling because 
of its tendency to split. Ideal equip¬ 
ment is a two-bladed pocket knife of 
good steel, a pocket hone or carburun- 
dum, and a generous supply of band- 
aids. The proper position of the hands 
in relation to the knife cannot be 
stressed too highly. However, very often 
the only lesson in safe whittling must 
come the hard way. 

There is much less risk in carving, 
since the work is done with mallet and 
chisel, on a larger piece of wood. For 
carving, three or four chisels, flat and 
gouge, will suffice, along with a mallet 
of wood or composition rubber. To keep 
wood chisels in good order, use three 
or more grades of oil stone. Carburun- 
dum is one of the best. 

The summer carving referred to in 
the opening paragraph was a nine-foot 
totem pole. The tree, felled by a hurri¬ 
cane, was cut, and stripped by Jack, 
one of our expert and ever-willing 
woodsmen. The pole was the extra¬ 


curricular project of our newest camper 
group, the “Shawnee”, who were 
formed this year from a subdivision of 
our oldest group. It was done entirely 
in secret. To begin with, a design was 
drawn up, telling the history of the 
new “tribe” in Indian symbobls. After 
this was applied to the pole, the camp¬ 
ers came en masse, with their counsel¬ 
lors, for demonstrations in the art of 
carving. From then on, each day at 
4:30 the “Shawnee” came in groups of 
three to the loft of the barn, where they 
worked until tea-time. The final result 
was erected late in August, in a newly 
built council ring. Every camper did a 
small part. They will never forget the 
pride which comes from a group 
achievement. 

Modelling, to turn from cutting away 
to building up, can be a lot of fun, 
and it can produce good results. A kiln, 
a supply of clay and basic glaze colours, 
and some home-made tools and acces¬ 
sories,. are all that is required to make 
Indian-style coil pottery, and simple 
pottery figures. Ceramics is, however, 
a rather highly technical and scientific 
craft to go into very deeply. Most 
waterfront camps have a supply of 
natural clay nearby. Usually this clay 
cannot be fired to a permanent state 
without a lot of refiring. It can be made 
semi-permanent, by the application on 
the dry clay of three coats of thin 
shellac, twenty-four hours apart, and 
a coat of enamel. 

Sketching, modelling and carving are 
a few of the forms that creative art 
can take. At camp it is in peril of being 
put aside for activities that appear more 
vital. Let us bear in mind that the first 
sign of civilization in ancient primitive 
man, came when he decorated his home, 
and his tools and equipment. We need 
creative art. Let us make a place for it. 
Its rewards will speak for themselves.

SHORT TERM CAMPING HAS LITTLE VALUE 


Short term camping is like trying to put out a fire with a toy water pistol. 
All you can do is touch the fringes of the fire lightly. Similarly, with short 
term camping, we only lightly touch the real potentials of camping. We give 
the camper glimpses of wonderful things that he might do, but we do not 
really offer him a chance to experience that matchless feeling of doing them. 

Long term camping is wise camping from two important aspects — the 
camper, and the staff. The camper achieves more of a variety of things, more 
thoroughly. He returns home with the satisfied feeling of having reached 
some anticipated goals. The staff person, on the other hand, has satisfaction 
in actually seeing results on the job, when he has time to share his experience 
with the camper. 

There is a caution on long term camping, which we should be aware 
of and that is: the term should not exceed the point where the learning 
process is slowed down to a walk. A good Camp Director can recognize this 
point in his staff as well as in his campers when they start to go a bit stale. 
However, with our short Canadian summers, we are not faced with this 
problem too seriously. Most camps are geared to provide good, snappy, two- 
week or one-month programmes for our campers. 

The Camping term should be long enough to allow the camper to adjust 
from the home routines to the new exciting camping life. Then, with his 
camp mates and staff friends, there should be time to try out new things, 
develop old skills, explore strange places and recognize the wonders of na¬ 
ture. All the while, a strong sense of citizenship will be taking hold on this 
young life. 

Yes, to transmit the real potential of camping to our young campers 
does take time. There is no “Reader’s Digest” technique for camping, to 
provide a well-rounded experience in living, that will stay with the camper. 
Through life, let us continue to provide the best in long term camping. 


26 


Canadian Camping 






ISSUES 


This month, the Issue about 
which out writers duel is: 
Short term vs. Long term 
Camping. 


THERE ARE REAL VALUES IN SHORT-TERM CAMPING 


Few would deny the many values of a four or eight-week camp period. 
To be away from the city and in a camp setting for that length of time, can 
be a very wonderful adventure in so many ways. But the two week camp 
has its values too. Perhaps the most obvious one is that it gives many child¬ 
ren whose families could not afford to send them to a four or eight-week 
camp, a chance to have a camp experience. Then too, there are groups that 
raise money to send needy or upset children to camp. The two-week camp 
period enables such groups to help more children, or, in some cases, to 
help at all, where the cost of a longer camp might be more than they could 
raise. 

Some would maintain that two weeks is not long enough for a child 
to become at home in the camp setting, or to learn more than a fraction of 
what he could learn in a longer camp. On the other hand, camp is a very 
tiring experience for many children. If they are young children, if they 
have never been away from home before, if they are nervous, excitable 

youngsters, the continual excitement and adventure of camp drain their 
energies so greatly that two weeks is long enough. 

Camp is important in a child’s summer — but so is the holiday with 
his family and the holiday at some pal’s home or summer place. The four 
or eight-week camp rules out other things for many children. The two- 
week camper often can fill the rest of his summer with a variety of ex¬ 
periences that can be as valuable for him — though in different ways — as 
his time at camp. 

Camp can be a magical experience that stays in a very special corner 
of a child’s memory. And perhaps this magic can be produced and sus¬ 
tained more easily in the shorter period. This is especially true in camp¬ 

sites that do not have the possibilities of the northern lakes and woods. Two 
weeks can be packed with fresh, new adventures and joys, and the child 

goes home before any trace of boredom or restlessness can creep in. 


Toronto, Canada, June , 1956

JUNIOR CAMP 


SOME SUGGESTIONS TO COUNSELLORS 
AND DIRECTORS WHO WORK WITH 
THE FIVE TO EIGHT YEAR OLDS 


E. Flynn 
Camp Oconto 


This is a child’s first experience away 
from home. This summer’s activity can 
make or mar him for life as far a,s camp¬ 
ing is concerned. It is possible for all 
counsellors to help him enjoy the 
happiest holiday of his young life, one 
he will want to repeat every year. 

Remember that camping for Juniors 
is a skill in itself. Programme must be 
geared to the age and endurance of the 
children, rather than being an adult 
programme superimposed on these tiny 
tots. 

House Juniors in cabins rather than 
in tents; (a) for comfort, good health, 


and easy control; (b) so that campers 
of this age can anticipate tent life in 
the more advanced sections. 

Equip those cabins with inside 
shutters to cover the screened windows, 
and to keep out damp draughts at 
night, when necessary. 

Build windows low enough that small 
campers can look outside easily, and 
large enough that every room can be 
well-aired. 

Use single beds, small enough to fit 
their size, rather than double bunks. 

Build a separate dining room for 
Juniors, so that they can eat at their 
own pace, and relax away from the 
hubbub of older children. If possible, 
feed them in two small groups at 
separate lunch hours, rather than in one 
large group. The smaller group is easier 
to control. 


30 


Canadian Camping 




Select counsellors who love small 
children, and who are willing to be on 
the alert twenty four hours of the day 
and night. 

Select counsellors who are not too 
voung . . . nor too old, for that matter. 
The younger the camper, the older the 
counsellor is a general rule. In other 
words, choose a mature, sympathetic 
person as counsellor, one who can have 
patience with small ones, one who can 
share the whimsical ideas and problems 
common to children of this age. 

Arrange swimming periods so that 
Juniors swim late in the morning and 
early in the afternoon, so that they will 
get maximum sunshine. 

Dress Juniors in slacks and sweater 
first thing in the morning when the air 
can be coolish until breakfast, espe¬ 
cially during Daylight Saving time. 
Comfortable campers are happy 
campers, especially early in the 
morning! 

Allow them to play on their own 
during free play periods; let them 
organize their own games as their first 
experience in learning the Give-and- 
Take everyday life demands. 

Provide a flexible programme so that 
it does not become strained or rushed 
or over-stimulated at any time. 

Prevent children becoming exhausted 
through too much activity over a long 
period of time. Alternate an active 
games programme with a relaxing activ¬ 
ity or a period of free play. 

If the weather changes don’t be 
afraid to adjust programme.*- If the 
children want to do someting other than 
you have planned, it’s fun to let them 
do as they please sometimes. 


Please don’t be rigid or regimented 
with the children or with programme. 
They are regimented all year, let camp 
be fun. If they make discoveries in 
nature, go along with them. If they 
need explanations or a discussion 
period, give it to them, and you will 
be pleased with the way they respond. 
The only activities they must be on 
time for are: swimming, riding, crafts, 
boating, any activity (or meals, of 
course) which affects the entire camp. 

See that they wear bathing caps for 
swimming, and sun hats on sunny days. 

Keep swimming periods short; and 
remove them from water the minute 
they show signs of cold . . . blue lips, 
shivering, “duck bumps.” 

Insist that they wear a beach robe or 
a large beach towel to the swimming 
area so that this can be put on as soon 
as they come from the water. 

Keep plenty of extra blankets on 
hand for chilly northern nights; let 
them wear sweaters and socks to bed 
too, if they wish. They keep campers 
warm, and warmth at night cuts down 
on bed-wetting, as well as chills which 
might lead to colds. 

Report any unsual symptom . . . skin 
rash, “sniffle”, sore ear or throat, cuts, 
a sudden listlessness ... to the doctor or 
nurse at once. At camp these simple 
complaints might be an indication of 
on-coming illness. 

Insist that Junior campers get a full 
rest period ... at least a full hour . . . 
after lunch. Put them in bed, in pyja¬ 
mas or shorts, covered with blanket 
(sheet' in hot weather). No comic 
books, colouring books or letter-writing 
in this section at rest hour. This is a 
time for sleep . . . and they will sleep!

Consider the following ideas for 
Junior Programme: — 

All kinds of picnics; treasure hunts; 
counsellor hunts of a simple variety; 
ITcIe-and-seek; simple and short “bush¬ 
whacking” jaunts. 

Marshmallow and pop-corn roasts, 
where they can roast and toast the food 
themselves, under close supervision, of 
course; Sing-songs around the bonfire; 
all sorts of action songs. 

Easy-for-them-to-do improvements to 
the camp site: with much supervision 
and guidance, simple transplanting of 
trees, making a new camp-fire ring; 
planting a garden with quickly-growing 
seeds; building a stone wall around a 
cabin or outlining paths with stones 
which could be whitewashed. 

Skit Nights; Topsy-Turvy Days 
(counsellors must dress up as well for 
this one!) Masquerades with activities 
—Town Fair, Church Picnic, Circus, 
Pirate Night. 

Crafts geared to Junior abilities: 
Plenty of plasticine; individual black¬ 
boards (about 20” X 24”) and a supply 
of coloured chalk; finger paints; paper 
weaving mats (of which they never 
tire) ; wax crayons (buy the Jumbo 
size which do not melt or bend) with 
plenty of paper for an art exhibit of 
their own! Raffia for small mats and 
serviette rings they can take home; 
plastic lacing for braiding belts or 
bracelets. 

If you are having a Special Event, 
always let them help decorate the room. 

Provide, if possible, swings, slides, 
sand boxes and any other playground 
equipment for the first few days of 
camp. 

.... and good camping to everybody!

—that high standards of neatness and 
tidiness should be encouraged at all 
times in cabins and throughout the 
camp generally. Thus we will at all 
times emphasize this as part of the 
responsibilities of camper and staff 
alike as well as administration. 

—that the use of awards and compe¬

standards of personal accomplish¬ 
ment as well as tidiness and neatness,

means of motivation and make every 
effort to have the camper experience 
the satisfaction that comes from co¬ 
operation and accepting responsibili¬ 
ties for the good of the whole group. 

—that health in its newest and broad¬ 
est concept is all important. Thus 
we will provide a high standard of 
meals, a healthful environment, 
safety without coddling, and every 
opportunity to have improved health, 
mentally and socially. 

—that there is a fundamental need for 
worship, irrespective of creed or 
color. Thus we will provide well 
planned and suitable chapel services, 
campfires, evening music and 
“drifts” and other types of pro¬ 
gramme which will meet this need.

CAMPFIRE TIME 


Kay McClelland, 

Section Head , 
Camp Oconto . 


“Just a song at twilight , when the lights are low, 
And the flickering shadows softly come and go” 


Perhaps nowhere do these words 
more aptly apply than to our camp¬ 
fires where we pause for fellowship 
before rest. There is magic in the mu¬ 
sic that drifts with the lazy smoke over 
the shimmering lake as young voices 
sweetly blend in camp songs. 

Tlie seeming spontaneity which 
marks a good campfire session is only 
accomplished through careful prepara¬ 
tion and planning by its leaders. Fol¬ 
lowing are a few principles which have 
proven successful: 

(1) One person should be in 
charge of all campfires. This leader 
should possess a vital personality, a 
good musical ear and a vivid imagina¬ 
tion. A skilled leader draws upon his 
co-workers for novel and refreshing 
ideas of presentation. Upon this 
leader falls the responsibility of pre¬ 
paring for a campfire. He must see that 
every counsellor knows the songs to be 
sung. During the actual campfire the 


counsellors’ strength and confidence in 
song will be most valuable. 

(2) The purpose and generaf outline 
of a campfire should be clearly out¬ 
lined to all staff members. The camp¬ 
fire is a time when the group comes 
together for a pleasurable experience. 
It is the climax to a busy day, so 
should begin with enthusiasm. Use 
campfire games, action and lively songs 
first, and then when the campers are 
warmed up insert a new song (if 
desired). The second portion of the 
campfire sets the mood required before 
the campers retire. Stories, and the 
quieter, lovelier melodies of the 
woods, lakes and fireside accomplish 
this aim. Closing with a vesper or Taps, 
the campers are relaxed and ready for 
a refreshing sleep. 

(3) Plan campfires in advance. By 
planning, there is less likelihood of 
repetition or confusion. Plan that one 
night the campfire will include chal¬ 
lenges, the next stunts, the next a 


34 


Canadian Camping 



theme of foreign lands and so on. One 
caution however — although prepared 
in advance, a campfire must be flexible. 

(4) Along with music which forms 
the major portion of a campfire, any 
number of additional items may be in¬ 
cluded : ceremonials, skits, challenges, 
tent turns, counsellor nights, dances, 
canoe trip reports, and stories name but 
a few. It is best to let the campers 
know ahead of time what type of 
campfire can be expected. They may 
then prepare themselves accordingly as 
to what songs they would like and so 
on. 

The Campfire Itself. 

Although the campfire may take on 
many themes it should always begin in 
the same manner. An appropriate, short 
fire-lighting ceremony and the round, 
“Fire’s Burning”, is most effective. 
Should a round be used at the open¬ 
ing of the campfire, divide your 
circle before beginning. Be sure there 
are a few strong voices in each section. 
(The circle is now divided for future 
rounds.) 

The fire lit, suggest a well known, 
rollicking song which will capture the 
enthusiasm of every camper. Perhaps 
“We are the Redmen”, “Six Little 
Ducks” or “My Paddle’s Keen and 
Bright” could be used. Now ask for 
requests. The campers will ask for their 
favourites time and time again. If the 
song is suitable and the majority en¬ 
joy singing it, use it. Don’t, however, 
allow the same song or songs to be 
sung all the time. Suggest something 
else in its place, pointing out that we 
sang that earlier, or yesterday. There 
will, of course, be some songs that 
are more popular than others and so 
sung more often, but that is a little 
different than having the same re¬ 
quests time after time. After a few 
requests and the campers are singing 
well, is the time to introduce a new 
song occasionally. 


When introducing a new song be 
sure to set a background whether true 
or fictitious. Perhaps the circumstances 
leading to your acquiring the song or 
a little about the country the song 
concerns, anything to set the mood. 
Now sing the song in an energetic, sure 
voice. Have a few counsellors help 
you if necessary, but know the song 
well enough that a paper or book is 
unnecessary. The campers now have 
the general idea of the song. The sec¬ 
ond time you sing it, have them listen 
for a certain part by asking a question, 
the answer to which is found within 
the lyrics. This step may be repeated 
but not too often. Have your group 
sing or hum as soon as possible. Only 
by repetition can they pick up the tune 
and words. Often, having the group 
repeat the words after you helps. 

Tips 

If it is a lengthy song do not try to 
complete it at the first campfire. The 
children are energetic and do not 
want to spend too much time on one 
song. A song may have to be reviewed 
every other night for a week or more 
before the campers are able to sing it 
with confidence. If it is a short song a 
new verse can be added at each camp¬ 
fire after the tune is learned. Unless 
exceptionally easy, do not try to sing 
a “round” as a round the first night. 
Be sure the campers know the tune 
and verse well before breaking into 
parts. 

Always follow a new song with one 
or more well known tunes. Perhaps 
“Old King Cole”, “Kookaberra” and 
“My Tall Silk Hat” would be good. It 
is now time for the special event. A story 
is always popular. The Tadger Tales, 
Indian Stories or Legends, are especially 
suitable. Read or tell it with enthusiasm 
and expression. The last energetic zest 
for activity has been satisfied, so we 
turn to a quieter atmosphere in prepa¬ 
ration for bed.

planning manifested itself in every 
phase of camp life. Not only were the 
summer months given over entirely to 
her camp family, but all who know 
Miss Percival intimately, appreciated 
her devotion during the entire year to 
the interests of camping. 

It is difficult to measure by any 
standard the amount of goodness which 
a life may impart. Certainly a richness 
m love of the out-of-doors, happy 
fellowship and pride in accomplishment 

_a richness immeasureable, has been 

the lot of the hundreds of campers and 
counsellors who have had the good 
fortune to come under Miss Percy’s 
direction at Ouareau. Safe and care¬ 
fully supervised activities, high health 
standards and the utmost comfort and 
happiness of all was her daily concern. 

To conclude, perhaps the greatest 
tribute that can be paid one of our 
finest camp directors is expressed in the 
words of one of her campers. “No 
camper could ever recall Ouareau with¬ 
out thinking of ‘Miss Percy’ with 
her amazing patience, kindness and 
thoughtfulness, and, last but not least, 
that wonderful smile for everyone.” 


A few songs such as Whip-poor- 
Will”. “Father Time”, and “Land of 
the Silverbirch”, help prepare the 
campers. The fire finally flickers low 
and the campers stand reverently for 
Vespers and Taps. 

In later years old campers often 
find their most cherished memories are 
those woven with the curling smoke 
of a campfire.

Svmethinp Biappens 
Amid LiiMtjhter and Simp 


Wendys and Susans and scores of 
others come to camp each summer, 
their heads still full of school with its 
pressures and standards, with its teach¬ 
ers, class-mates and homework not yet 
forgotten. The counsellor sees these 
children arrive at camp, some aglow 
with keen (expectancy, some with a 
glimmer of uncertainty, some boldly en¬ 
thusiastic, others shyly anticipating 
their new venture — or perhaps the 
term ‘adventure’ would be more apt; 
for surely it is an adventure to be go¬ 
ing to camp, to live next to Nature, to 
acquire new skills and make new 
friends. As they arrive some seem 
alone, bewildered perhaps, or just tak¬ 
ing stock of the situation; others bunch 
together laughing and chattering, re¬ 
newing old friendships and meeting 
new companions. 

As if by magic, summer days flash 
by and soon it is time to return home. 
The counsellor watches these same 
children leave, their camping days 
over for another year — but are they 
really the same children? Wendy has 
grown a full two inches, Susan’s hair 
is three shades lighter, bleached by a 
summer’s sun. Their skins are bronzed 
and their bodies firm and sturdy. On 
closer inspection, that one over there, 
leaning on her paddle, has a look of 
assurance, where once there was shy 
hesitance; this one’s eyes sparkle with 
a new lustre, the result of happy ex¬ 
perience and shared pleasures. A few 
still stand alone, but even their soli¬ 
tude has changed from bewilder¬ 
ment to confidence; very often behind 
it lie dreams and aspirations to be ful- 


Carolyn M. Schmidt 

Institute of Child Study,, 
Toronto. 


filled another summer. Each group has 
enlarged now and the individual child¬ 
ren in it have altered, although they 
themselves may not even realize this. 
Each has learned something from be¬ 
ing at camp: some a little, some a great 
deal. Among the changes wrought may 
be improved outlook, a better adjust¬ 
ment to group living, or a growth in 
knowledge and stature due to leader¬ 
ship training and the assumption of 
responsibility. Whatever the changes 
may be, these campers return home dif¬ 
ferent children, physically and mentally 
healthier as a result of their camping 
experience. 

The question now arises what has 
brought about these changes and how 
have these new learnings been ac¬ 
quired? Primarily, the atmosphere in a 
camping situation is the essential fac¬ 
tor. In a good camp, children feel free 
from strain and tension. When they are 
tired it is a healthy tiredness. They live, 
laugh, play and work together in both 
large and small groups, yet learn to 
respect each other’s individuality. The 


38 


Canadian Camping 




activities of school and city-life find 
little place in the naturalness and 
simplicity of the outdoors. Children can 
relax and be their best selves. At camp, 
children strive for accomplishment, be 
it the dog-paddle or a swan dive; sail¬ 
ing a boat alone, or just helping to 
hoist sails: learning the basic canoe¬ 
ing strokes or striving to attain the 
perfection of an expert. In this set¬ 
ting, their days are well-spent in 
wholesome play and purposeful acti¬ 
vity in a relaxed atmosphere. 

There are dozens of opportunities in 
a camping situation for participation 
in such group activities as council-fires, 
cabin entertainment nights, sing-songs, 
musicales and dramatic productions. 
Nevertheless creativity and originality 
have many outlets, too: in the craft 
shop, on sketching expeditions, making 
up skits, and improvising costumes lor 
a masquerade or play. Even the simplest 
contribution can add something to camp 
life, however small and insignificant it 
may seem. Perhaps it may be only a 
contagious laugh, an encouraging smile 
for someone who needs it, or an en- 
thsiasm that is catching. 

The effect of camping on behaviour 
adjustment and social development can 
be considerable. Through experiences 
in harmonious living, campers learn to 
accept their share of responsibility, to 
cooperate with others, and to grow 
in unselfishness. The child learns to 
do things in a group, and out of con¬ 
sideration for the group. Some learn 
too, the satisfaction of momentary soli¬ 
tude and of just sitting and thinking for 
a while; still others learn for the first 
time what it is to have fun for fun’s 
sake. The counsellor i.s always at hand 
to instruct and encourage the camp¬ 
ers in every undertaking. An uncertain 
child frequently develops confidence in 
the realization that there is someone 
who has faith in his ability, and be¬ 
gins to feel that he ‘belongs’ in camp. 



Many children who find themselves 
at camp and away from their families, 
gain in self reliance and in learn¬ 
ing to make decisions for themselves; 
at the same time, interests are broad¬ 
ened and judgment acquired. Through¬ 
out the camper’s day many decisions 
must be made to be punctual or late, 
to be tidy or untidy, to persevere or 
to take a defeatist attitude; to con¬ 
centrate exclusively on one activity or 
to develop various skills; to participate 
in an activity or to be an onlooker. 
Through their choices, they ex¬ 
perience success or failure, satisfaction 
or dissatisfaction, depending on their 
own attitudes. Often the help and en¬ 
couragement of fellow-campers and a 
counsellor’s friendly interest can stimu¬ 
late desirable choices and attitudes. 
Of course, being away from family in 
this new way of living requires a de¬ 
gree of emotional, physical and social 
maturity. The child may miss the 
whole value of camp life if he is sent 
before he is ready.

Toronto , Canada , June , 1956

Trips and 

Campcraft 

Kirk Wipper, 

Department of Physical and Health Education, 

University of Toronto. 


The purpose of this article is to out¬ 
line the value of tripping and campcraft 
from three points of view. First, why 
these activities are a significant part of 
the camp programme; secondly, what 
additional emphases might be made 
to increase the value of these activities, 
and, finally, how this experience in 
camping can be effected with the most 
desirable results. 

In a recent issue of a camping maga¬ 
zine the following statement was made: 

“Deep in the hearts of all sports¬ 
men is the dream of a wilderness trip, 
an expedition that will give them the 
opportunity to follow the water trails 
and portages of voyageurs and relieve 
at least in part, those days when man 
would fill his food pack with a bag of 
flour, salt, bacon (fat) and tea, and 
set out for many weeks’ trip into 
the bush, confident in his ability to 
live off the laijd and return to 
civilization in better shape than when 
he left.” 

It should be quite obvious that we 
cannot submit ourselves, or our young¬ 
sters, to this kind of primitive camping 
as we strive to build an experience 
which will always remain with us as a 
happy one. Nor is it necessary to sub¬ 
mit to such privation to enjoy the 
advantages of the adventure inherent in 
this integral part of the camp pro¬ 


gramme. With proper planning and 
organization the “dream” mentioned 
above should be placed within the 
reach of participants, but certainly in 
a framework which fits the interests, 
needs and capabilities of the campers. 

It may seem superfluous to mention 
in the first place that tripping in its 
broadest sense (on foot, by canoe, on 
horseback, by bicycle, etc.) and camp¬ 
craft provide an extraordinary oppor¬ 
tunity for fun, for sheer enjoyment. This 
can only be true if the tripping guide 
and the campcraft counsellor has not 
dampened such a possibility by domina¬ 
tion of the undertaking, by disregard 
for such factors a§ fatigue of campers 
or their natural interests, or by failing 
to appreciate camp objectives in this 
kind of programming. 

The expansion of horizons, the 
participation in a sense of wholesome 
adventure are further by-products of 
close association with the natural en¬ 
vironment encouraged through camp¬ 
craft and tripping. And, during these 
pioneering pursuits the lure of the 
unexpected urges campers to adjust to 
and communicate with the changing 
environment. This should culminate in 
an uplifting of the spirit and a refresh¬ 
ing of the mind. An alert guide and 
counsellor should submit to this ex¬ 
perience himself and perhaps share it 
with his fellow travellers and campers. 


40 


Canadian Camping 



As campers explore into each new area 
of beauty and quiet, and have as their 
companions things which are of ever¬ 
lasting significance, it would seem that 
discussions of desirable spiritual power 
should take place with good result. 
Adjustment to others, to the environ¬ 
ment and to the requirements of trip 
or project is a value that must not be 
overlooked. Most campers soon discover 
that their own welfare is directly de¬ 
pendent on the contribution of each 
member of the group. Here is a 
situation in which sincerity of effort is 
important. And it is a wise trip leader 
who will take advantage of these 
activities to show developing human 
beings the necessity for teamwork and 
compatability. 

In these activities campers have a 
splendid situation in which to cultivate 
initiative and resourcefulness. This is 
part of the adjustment that must 
continually be made by campers, 
particularly in tripping. It is a matter 
of resolving the many little problems 
that should arise as campers strive to 
live in and out of doors with comfort, 
health and safety. This demands 
restraint on the part of the counsellor, 
who should with all the wisdom he 
can acquire deliberately undertake to 
give such responsibility to campers 
within their capacity. Self reliance on 
one’s own skill and judgment stands 
as another worthy value. 

To carry on at some length in this 
brief consideration of why the activities 
of tripping and campcraft are valuable 
in the camp programme should not be 
difficult, for such is the stature of the 
topic. For example little or no reference 
has been made to comradeship, to build¬ 
ing lasting memories of high calibre, to 
learning the simple rules of living, or 
to realizing such ordinary things as the 
necessity for care of equipment. To 
make these aspects of programming 
valuable, thought is required in estab-

lishing objectives. In setting these up it 
is necessary to clearly recognize why the 
activity is worth such attention in the 
first place. 

Some of the ways in which tripping 
and campcraft are valuable have been 
outlined. The next step is to list some 
things which may stimulate the trip 
counsellor, or the campcraft counsellor, 
to make this part of camp programme- 
ing more worth while. 

1. Star Study—not just the names of 
stars, but their relation to this, and 
other planets, the patterns they 
suggest, their importance in navi¬ 
gation, etc. 

2. Photography and Art. 

3. Orienteering and exploring. 

4. Improvement of swimming and 
water safety knowledge. 

5. Weather—an understanding of 
what causes certain conditions and 
ability to appraise future status. 

6. Music and singing. 

7. Discussions 

8. Wildlife lore 

9. Map making and reading—with 
orienteering 

10. Morning inspirations and evening 
campfires (informal) 

11. Story telling, legends, history 

12. Cooking 

13. Fishing 

14. Collections—natural objects or col¬ 
lecting materials for creative crafts 

15. Building outposts or other facilities 
for future trips, or carrying out a 
service of some kind to trails and 
campsites, i.e. new portages. 

It is recognized that these accessory 
type activities would depend on the 
type of trip being taken, the age and 
capacity of the campers, as well as their 
general experience in camping. 

Finally, the interest of those concern¬ 
ed with this aspect of camp programme 
must be focused on methods which will 




42 


Canadian Camping 










permit the most desirable product from 
these activities. At the outset it should 
be clear that camper participation is of 
utmost importance. If experience re¬ 
sulting from the camper’s effort is to be 
of greatest value, this aim must be 
pursued with patience and sincerity. 
Early in the preparation for specific 
activities within these categories a pur¬ 
pose for the particular experience 
should be defined. Exactly what will be 
the result of the enterprise and how 
can it best be accomplished? Of course, 
purpose and technique must be consist¬ 
ent with the policy of the camp. This 
requirement will involve the judgment 
of other staff members who will supple¬ 
ment the contribution of the direct par¬ 
ticipants — the campers. 

At this stage motivation is important. 
Some campers will express an interest 
on their own. They will need little more 
than guidance in making proper pre¬ 
paration. Others will require assistance 
in overcoming a natural fear of the un¬ 
expected. This applies directly to trip¬ 
ping and perhaps only in a very minor 
way to campcraft. The danger here is 
that the immature counsellor may not 
understand the purpose of an outing 
away from camp and motivate campers 
falsely for his own benefit. The quali¬ 
fied trip director can avoid this situa¬ 
tion by helping camp personnel to 
appreciate the scope and nature of 
these activities — the proper perspective 
for such activities. 

It is a wise trip or campcraft director 
who permits some leeway in a specific 
project to allow for particular oppor¬ 
tunities which may arise or for un¬ 
foreseen difficulties. This does lend 
itself to creative thinking and decision, 
demanded by the nature of the situa¬ 
tion. It must be added that the success 
of such technique is dependent upon 
previous experience at camp or in 
earlier lead-up activities.

STORIES FOR JUNIOR WORSHIP 

In Three Books by Alice Greer Kelsey, 
STORIES FOR JUNIOR WOR¬ 
SHIP, STORIES FOR GROWING, 
and THE TEAKWOOD PULPIT 
AND OTHER STORIES, each con¬ 
tains from 30 to 35 stories, any one 
of which would take from 5 to 10 
minutes to read aloud or to retell in 
your own words. A kernel of wisdom, 
a Christian principle, are to be found 
at the heart of each colourful story. 
Mrs. Kelsey has gathered her tales 
from all over the world, from today 
and yesterday, from history, from 
folk lore, from nature, and from per¬ 
sonal experience. Many of them begin 
with “Once upon a time. .” She has 
grouped them in her three books under 
headings such as ‘Stories of World Un¬ 
derstanding 5 , ‘Stories of Men We Ad¬ 
mire 5 , ‘Stories of the Holidays 5 , ‘Stories 
of the Out-of-Doors 5 , ‘Boys and Girls 
Today. 5 

As we observed in discussing Mary 
S. Edgar’s UNDER OPEN SKIES in 
the February issue, Jesus the Great 
Teacher chose the parable or story 
through which to tell His listeners 
about God and the good life. It has 


far more impact than talking in a 
general way about being kind or honest 
or brave. Imagination is a faculty that 
needs developing if we are to under¬ 
stand other people or sec the chal¬ 
lenge of life around us; it will prompt 
us to be warm and personal and cre¬ 
ative about our Christian acts. Mrs. 
Kelsey’s stories touch off that spark 
of imagination and give it direction. 
Do you remember reading in The 
Book of Knowledge as a youngster 
the various series of stories — The 
Book of Wonder, The Book of Golden 
Deeds — and how exciting some of 
them were? Maybe it is rather incon¬ 
gruous that, growing up in the middle 
of the prairies, I liked best to imagine 
myself as Grace Darling, staunchly 
rowing the rescue boat while the 
waves crashed about the lighthouse! 
The story made it urgent to me to 
learn how to manage a boat (I did 
so in Ontario a few years later!) 
and to learn first aid — to be pre¬ 
pared when the call should come. In 
this way, Mrs. Kelsey’s stories are de¬ 
signed to arouse the imagination of 
young people to find the adventure 
in Christian living. Abingdon Press. 
(In Canada, G. R. Welsh & Go., To¬ 
ronto.) $2 each.

OUTDOORS WITH PETE 
McGILLEN 

He is unique in that he is Canada’s 
only Outdoors Editor on a metropoli¬ 
tan daily; he is a Life Member of 
five, and Honorary Member of nine 
Rod and Gun Clubs of Ontario; he is 
the most widely quoted Outdoors writer 
in Canada, and a speaker who is book¬ 
ed in advance from one year’s end to 
the other. All that and a book, too 
. . . one that gives invaluable snippets 
of information, written to hold the 
interest of the youngest camper and 
keep him or her abreast of naturelore 
times. Mr. McGillen tells of the 
dangers of snapping turtles and ex¬ 
pounds on the bass, the pike and the 
salmon; through him his readers will 
learn why our parks should be pro¬ 
tected, why a bear is Public Enemy 
No. 1, and why we should make it 
our business to know more about wild 
life management. The Ryerson Press, 
Toronto. $3.50. 


HOW TO MAKE A MINIATURE 
ZOO 

Winson Brown. 

The intriguing habits of fish, ani¬ 
mals, birds and insects never cease to 
enthrall our small fry, to say nothing 
of their parents or counsellors, and 
it is on this premise that Mr. Brown 
uses his book to explain how to col¬ 
lect and manage all sorts of small live 
animals. Starting with the plan of the 
zoo, he offers six different kinds for 
inspiration, suggests perfection in its 
presentation, good care of its inhabi¬ 
tants, and, if possible, a display room 
housing no other exhibits or hobbies. 
‘This book can only start you out as a 
zoo keeper,” he says. ‘Patience, gentle¬ 
ness, study, and above all good habits 
of feeding and cleaning will gradually 
turn you into an experienced keeper 
who overcomes these difficulties’. Little, 
Brown & Co. (Canada), Limited, To¬ 
ronto 16. $3.

Swimming pools should comply with 
the Provincial Regulations governing 
their construction and operation. 
Natural waters should meet generally 
accepted bacteriological standards, and 
be free of any significant local pollution. 

Miscellaneous 

Laundry operations must not be 
carried out in the natural waters about 
the camp. An active maintenance and 
good housekeeping programme is 
essential. 

The use of fly sprays and screens is 
important in the fly control programme 
along with the control of any breeding 
grounds. 

Summary 

In brief summation, the inspector 
looks for a combination of satisfactory 
operations and physical layout in a 
sanitary environment.

continued from page 43 

All plans and purpose of the trip 
should be clearly outlined to the camp 
director. There should be a two-way 
confidence. Campers should be confi¬ 
dent that they can carry through a 
proposed project well and the director 
of the camp should feel that the par¬ 
ticipants and the staff personnel of 
the trip will conduct themselves wisely. 
For example the director should know 
the route and overnight camping places; 
he should also know that the trip will 
not venture out in a severe storm in 
order to make a deadline. 

Finally, it is good technique to evalu¬ 
ate the trip. Was the purpose of the trip 
well defined for this group of camp¬ 
ers? Did each participant gain some¬ 
thing truly significant? Was the me¬ 
thod chosen lor carrying out the 
project suitable? If done again how 
would it be improved? From the point 
of view of the counsellor and trip 
director there are these and other 
evaluations to be made in terms of 
knowledge gained of the camper. This 
latter should be recorded in confiden¬ 
tial files. On future projects such in¬ 
formation will be extremely valuable 
in providing a different experience 
which will meet a need defined by ob¬ 
servations made in previous endeavours. 

Perhaps some of us remember the 
story of a small girl who innocently 
annoyed her father who was intent 
upon reading the evening newspaper. 
He decided to occupy her by cutting 
up a map of the world that he found 
in a magazine, and challenging her 
to piece it together. This idea she 
promptly accepted. Soon, to his amaze¬ 
ment, she returned with the task well 
done. “How did you ever do that?” 
he asked. “Oh”, she replied, “It was 
easy. I saw a large picture of a boy 
on the other side and if you put the 
boy together right, the world comes 
out fine”. 

This is our challenge for camping.

Canadian Camping 








continued from page 39 


Life in the outdoors offers much to 
those who are eager to learn. Camp¬ 
ers discover how comfortable a bed on 
the ground can be. They experience the 
joys of cooking on an open fire; they 
make toast over the coals and blend 
voices in companionship as their 
paddles carry them from lake to lake on 
canoe trips. They feel' the thrill of 
trundling across a portage and perhaps 
meeting a deer or a porcupine on the 
way. Theirs is the opportunity to gain 
knowledge about a multitude of things; 
to pick out the patterns in the star- 
filled sky as they lie under it; how to 
identify plants and the various spe¬ 
cies of pine, birch and cedar — and 
which to use when building a fire; 
about the animals, birds and fish — 
the wildlife whose presence is ever ap¬ 
parent in most camps’ surroundings. 
Through this direct contact with Na¬ 
ture’s wonders, not a few are imbued 
with a genuine and lasting aesthetic ap¬ 
preciation. 

The enduring effects left with each 
camper differ in themselves, almost as 
much as the hundreds of children who 
have gone to camp. But from the ex¬ 
perience of the many campers of past 
and present generations some signifi¬ 
cant things, in addition to the physic¬ 
al skills, are retained by nearly every 
one:— a sincere love ojf our special 
Canadian heritage, The Outdoors; 
memories of winding waterways and 
windswept lakes, quiet forest glens 
and mist-shrouded hills of dawn, the 
flaming sky of sunset: and possibly the 
most beloved of all — the camp-fire. 
To some of us, every fire we light 
brings to mind days filled with ac¬ 
tivity in rain or shine, days spent in 
happy comradeship and echoing with 
laughter and song.
